senses.def: collective for a group of animals
senses.comment: In a number of languages a ‘herd’ must be translated merely as ‘many,’ since there is frequently no corresponding collective term which would be applicable only or even primarily to pigs. In some languages, however, there are highly specific terms for various types of groups of animals, so that a distinctive collective expression may be used for pigs, sheep, horses, camels, etc.

senses.def: body of water between Italy and the Balkan peninsula
one who has been taken captive in war
senses.comment: In Luke 4:18 αἰχμάλωτος occurs on two levels: (1) in the literal sense of ‘being a captive of war’ and (2) in the broader sense of referring to all those who are oppressed by foreign domination.

senses.def: to catch fish, whether by means of a line or by a net
to cast a net in order to catch fish
senses.comment: The net implied in the use of the verb ἀμφιβάλλω was probably a circular net which had small weights on its edge and which could be thrown by a single person.

senses.def: the process of being taken up
to be caused to move by the wind
glosses: to be driven or carried about by the wind

senses.def: speak against something or someone
to move away from one place to another
to be absent from a place at a particular time
to cause someone’s death, normally by violent means, with or without intent and with or without legal justification
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀποκτείνω[a] ‘to kill,’ 20.61) to cause a state to cease, with the implication of strong emphasis and forceful action
senses.comment: In Ephesians 2:16 there is a subtle rhetorical device employed in ascribing to Christ the activity of ‘killing,’ when in reality he was the one who was killed on the cross in order to make life possible.

senses.def: a Christian woman, probably the wife of Philemon
a chief or highly important angel
senses.comment: An archangel may be described as ‘one who commands other angels’ or ‘a leading angel’ or ‘a chief angel.’

senses.def: pertaining to a state of safety and security, and hence free from danger
senses.comment: In Acts 16:23 ἀσφαλῶς does not refer to the safety of the prisoners but to the security with which they were guarded, hence eliminating any danger of their escaping.

senses.def: pertaining to being certain and thus completely believable

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to an extremely short period of time between a previous state or event and a subsequent state or event (in a number of contexts there is the implication of unexpectedness; but this seems to be a derivative of the context as a whole and not a part of the meaning of the lexical items)
pertaining to a king
senses.comment: The expression ‘his royal robes’ may be rendered as ‘his clothing which he had as king,’ and the phrase ‘the royal priesthood’ may be rendered as ‘priests who are like kings.’

senses.def: (ου n) the dwelling of a king or ruler; usually larger and more elaborate than the dwelling of an average person
senses.comment: In Luke 7:25 βασίλειον may be rendered as ‘the home of a king’ or ‘the home of a ruler.’

senses.def: to speak against someone in such a way as to harm or injure his or her reputation (occurring in relation to persons as well as to divine beings)
senses.comment: One way in which βλασφημέω and βλασφημία[a] were used in speaking of defaming God was by claiming some kind of equality with God. Any such statement was regarded by the Jews of biblical times as being harmful and injurious to the nature of God.

senses.def: a Macedonian companion of Paul
a Christian from Derbe
a man from Corinth who was baptized by Paul
the recipient of 3 John
pertaining to that which is known
pertaining to being well known or well acquainted with
senses.comment: It may also be possible to understand γνωστός in Luke 2:44 as meaning ‘friend’ (see 34.17).

senses.def: pertaining to being well known or famous because of some outstanding quality
senses.comment: For another interpretation of γνωστός in Acts 4:16, see γνωστός[f] 58.55.

senses.def: pertaining to being able to be known
senses.comment: In a number of languages the phrase ‘can be known,’ expressing a capacity relating to a passive state, must be restructured in an active form. This may often be done by rendering Romans 1:19 as ‘because what people can know about God is clearly evident to these persons’ or ‘they can clearly comprehend what they can know about God’ or ‘because they can clearly see what people can know about God.’

senses.def: pertaining to being a friend or acquaintance of someone, and thus enjoying certain privileges as a result of such a relation
senses.comment: It is clear that in John 18:15 γνωστός implies much more than simply being ‘well known by.’ To have been simply well known by the High Priest could have been a source of danger for the disciple. It was the fact of a relationship of friendship which made it possible for the disciple to view the proceedings.

senses.def: pertaining to that which is unusual in the sense of being extraordinary
senses.comment: For another interpretation of γνωστός in Acts 4:16, see γνωστός[c] 28.32.

senses.def: an extreme point on a scale involving negative values
to succeed someone as the owner of a particular object or possession
to continue in a particular state or condition unto the end

senses.subdomain: Double, Four Times As Much, Etc. [Multiples]
senses.def: twice the quantity
senses.comment: It is possible that in some contexts διπλοῦς does not mean precisely ‘twice as much’ but simply ‘much more.’ For example, in Revelation 18:6 it may be appropriate to translate ‘pay her back much more for what she has done.’

senses.def: pertaining to that which is difficult to accomplish or do
senses.comment: In some languages it may be difficult to render concisely the expression ‘only with difficulty.’ To express this contrastive element in connection with entering the kingdom of heaven, one must often translate as ‘a rich person will be able to enter into the kingdom of heaven, but it will be very difficult for him to do so.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (derivative of ἔθνος ‘nation,’ 11.55) pertaining to one who is not a Jew
pertaining to being handed over to someone
a position not contained within a particular area
the outside surface of an object
senses.comment: The manner in which ἔξωθεν[c], ἐκτός[b], and ὄπισθεν[c] may be rendered in particular contexts depends very largely upon what is being spoken about. For example, ἔξωθεν in 1 Peter 3:3 refers to the outward aids employed in making oneself beautiful, but instead of speaking of such objects as being on the surface or on the outside, it may be necessary to speak of those things which one puts on the body or what one wears.

senses.def: a marker of a contrast involving an exception
a marker of dissociation in the sense of being independent from someone or something
to go into or onto, as in the case of a boat
senses.comment: In certain contexts ἐμβαίνω[a] occurs without a specific indication of a ship or boat in the immediate context, for example, πάλιν ἐμβὰς ἀπῆλθεν εἰς τὸ πέραν ‘again embarking, he left for the other side’ Mark 8:13.|In a number of languages it is necessary to introduce into the context some specific reference to a boat or ship.

senses.def: to step into some area
senses.comment: This meaning is only found as a variant reading: ὁ οὖν πρῶτος ἐμβὰς μετὰ τὴν ταραχὴν τοῦ ὕδατος ὑγιὴς ἐγίνετο ‘the first one to go into (the pool) after the water was stirred up was healed’ John 5:3 (apparatus).

senses.def: to conceal oneself or to proceed secretly, while waiting for an appropriate opportunity to attack
glosses: to make plans for a secret attack
senses.comment: Since ambushing is such a widespread method of warfare and private attack, there is usually little or no difficulty involved in finding an appropriate term and using it in what might be called an anticipatory sense, that is to say, the employment of an ambush despite the fact that it was not finally successful.

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἐνεδρεύω[a] ‘to lie in ambush,’ to lie in wait in order to attack, 39.51) to plan, with the specific purpose of harming
cardinal number, where there are six hundred instances of a countable entity
senses.comment: The symbolic number in Revelation 13:18 would result from the total of the numerical values of the letters of the person’s name.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: an indefinite point or points of time, which may be roughly simultaneous to or overlap with another point of time (ὅταν[a] and ἐπάν may also imply some degree of uncertainty)
greatly desiring to do or have something
senses.comment: The phrase ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐπεθύμησα may be regarded as a type of Semitic idiom.

senses.def: strongly desiring to have what belongs to someone else and/or to engage in an activity which is morally wrong
pertaining to that which poses danger
to consume food, usually solids, but also liquids
senses.comment: As noted in the contexts of Matthew 12:1 and 1 Corinthians 9:7, ἐσθίω[a] is generic in the sense that it includes the consumption of both solid foods and liquids, but ἐσθίω is not employed in referring to the drinking of alcoholic beverages (see μεθύω[b] to drink freely of wine or beer, 23.37).|In some languages an important distinction is made in terms for ‘eating’ depending upon whether the eating is done by an adult or by a very small child, who in most instances must be helped to eat. Other distinctions in terminology for eating may involve the quantities of food (whether small or extensive), the rapidity with which one eats (gulping or mincing), the state of what is eaten (raw, fresh, cooked) or the type of food, for example, meat, cereal, fruit, or leafy vegetable.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἐσθίω[a] ‘to eat,’ 23.1) to destroy, with the implication of doing away with all traces of an object
(an idiom, literally: to eat one’s own bread) to earn a living by one’s own efforts
a castrated male person
senses.comment: In the ancient Middle East eunuchs were frequently in charge of royal harems and sometimes rose to high positions of state. The reference to the eunuch in Acts 8:34 is best interpreted as ‘court official’ (see 37.85).|Since in many societies castration of human males is not known, any attempt to employ a descriptive explanation within the text might seem unnecessarily crude and even vulgar. A number of translators have therefore preferred to borrow a term for eunuch and then place the explanation of its meaning in a glossary or word list.

senses.def: a human male who without being castrated is by nature incapable of sexual intercourse
a male person who abstains from marriage without being necessarily impotent
an official of an Oriental court who was entrusted with various important responsibilities and who was also a eunuch
senses.comment: In a context such as Acts 8:34, the focus of meaning of εὐνοῦχος[d] seems to be upon the person’s official responsibilities and position rather than upon his physical condition. It may therefore be more in keeping with the context to employ an expression such as ‘official of the court’ or ‘important official.’ On the other hand, in view of a eunuch’s limited acceptance in Jewish religion, the mention of the physical condition would fit Luke’s theological purposes well.

senses.def: to be in existence, having life, not dead
senses.comment: In some figurative expressions ζάω[a] and ζωή may involve serious complications in reference. For example, in John 6:51 the expression ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος ὁ ζῶν ‘I am the living bread’ may be understood in some languages as bread which has some living objects in it, namely, bread which is being eaten by worms or weevils. It may therefore be necessary to say ‘I am that bread which gives life.’|In a number of languages there is no noun-like word for ‘life.’ It may therefore be necessary to change all passages which speak of ‘life’ into a corresponding expression using a verb-like form meaning ‘to live.’

senses.def: to come back to life after having once died
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is a difficulty involved in formulating some expression for ‘resurrection’ or ‘living again,’ since such a phrase may refer to what is technically known as metempsychosis, that is to say, the rebirth of the soul in another existence, a belief which is widely held in a number of areas of south Asia. This problem may be avoided in some languages by speaking of ‘his body will live again’ or ‘his body will come back to life’ or ‘he will be the same person when he lives again.’

senses.def: to conduct oneself, with the particular manner specified by the context
senses.comment: In 2 Timothy 3:12 ζάω does not refer to physiological existence, but rather to the manner in which a person behaves or conducts himself in relationship to other persons and to God.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to experience worse treatment
to experience defeat and subjection
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘to be defeated’ is simply ‘to be conquered.’ In some instances this is expressed as ‘to become the prisoner of’ or idiomatically ‘to be led away by.’

senses.def: to observe something with continuity and attention, often with the implication that what is observed is something unusual
to come to understand as the result of perception
to experience an event or state, normally in negative expressions indicating what one will not experience
pertaining to being the exclusive property of someone
pertaining to that which is peculiar or distinctive to some entity

senses.subdomain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About
senses.def: a reference to each one individually

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: persons who in some sense belong to a so-called reference person
(an idiom, literally: according to that which is private) pertaining to what occurs in a private context or setting, in the sense of not being made known publicly
pertaining to one who is like or similar to an angel

senses.subdomain: Assign to a Role or Function
senses.def: to assign to someone a position of authority over others
senses.comment: ‘To put someone in charge of someone else’ may be expressed in a number of languages as ‘to give someone the authority to command others’ or ‘to say to someone, You are to give orders to others.’

senses.def: to cause a state to be
to lead or to bring down
a Christian of Troas
to think about, with the purpose of ultimate understanding
to rule or reign by exercising authority over

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: uppermost part of the human body, or the front or upper part of the body of an animal, typically separated from the rest of the body by a neck, and containing the brain, mouth, and sense organs; associated with the entire person, that person’s life and responsibilities
senses.comment: In some languages it may be necessary to distinguish clearly between the head which is still a part of a body and a severed head. It is this latter meaning which is obviously involved in Mark 6:25.|In rendering 1 Corinthians 11:4, πᾶς ἀνὴρ προσευχόμενος ἢ προφητεύων κατὰ κεφαλῆς ἔχων ‘any man who prays or prophesies with his head covered,’ it may be important to indicate that the covering is not one which is designed to cover the entire head including the face, but only the top of the head. The same applies, of course, to 1 Corinthians 11:5 and 1 Corinthians 11:7.

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of κεφαλή[a] ‘head,’ 8.10) one who is of supreme or pre-eminent status, in view of authority to order or command
glosses: one who is the head of

senses.def: (a set phrase, literally: head of the corner) the cornerstone or capstone of a building, essential to its construction (κεφαλὴ γωνίας occurs in the NT only figuratively in reference to Christ)
senses.comment: Though some scholars have thought that κεφαλὴ γωνίας refers to a keystone of an arch or the lintel stone over a door, it is highly probable that κεφαλὴ γωνίας has essentially the same meaning as ἀκρογωνιαῖος.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to lay down the head) to experience the rest which comes from sleep
senses.comment: ὁ δὲ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἔχει ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνω ‘the Son of Man has no place to lie down to rest’ Matthew 8:20, implies that Jesus possessed no permanent home. In John 19:30 this same expression must be understood not as an idiom but as a case of literally bowing the head (see 16.16).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to have down on the head) to wear a covering over one’s head

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the entire digestive apparatus, including stomach and intestines

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the uterus
(figurative extension of meaning of κοιλία[a] ‘belly,’ 8.67) the psychological faculty of desire, intent, and feeling
senses.comment: Though some persons have attempted to distinguish between σπλάγχνον[b], κοιλία[c], and νεφρός, it is extremely doubtful whether this is really possible or practical. The semantic focus in the use of these terms is clearly the deeper and more intimate feelings and emotions. In some languages one can use a term which literally means ‘belly’ or ‘bowels,’ but more often than not, these emotions are associated with some particular organ of the body such as heart, spleen, liver, etc. Rather, however, than attempting to employ a figurative expression which may or may not be fully equivalent, it is often preferable to refer to the emotional content by using terms such as ‘feelings,’ ‘intents,’ ‘desires,’ or ‘compassion,’ depending upon the context.

senses.def: desire for gratification of the body
senses.comment: It is also possible that κοιλία in Romans 16:18 refers to Jewish dietary laws and regulations.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the womb carries) to experience the process of pregnancy
senses.comment: It may, however, be necessary in some languages to render Luke 11:27 as ‘fortunate is the woman who gave you birth,’ since a literal reference to carrying in the womb may seem unduly crude.

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: decorative tassel attached to the bottom edge of a long outer garment
senses.comment: The edge of the garment designated by κράσπεδον[a] could have been plain or decorated. In Matthew 23:5 κράσπεδον denotes the tassels worn at the four corners of the outer garment (see 6.194). It is also possible that in all instances in which κράσπεδον is used in reference to Jesus’ clothing, the reference may be specifically to the tassels and not merely to the fringe or edge of the garment. The interpretation of such passages depends upon how strictly Jesus may have followed the Mosaic law and the manner in which the authors may have understood the meaning of κράσπεδον.

senses.def: the tassels which Jews were obliged to wear on the four corners of the outer garment (see)
senses.comment: In some languages tassels may be described as ‘decorated corners’ or ‘ribbons at the corners.’ See the discussion at 6.180.

senses.def: (a title for God and for Christ) one who exercises supernatural authority over mankind (see also 37.51)
senses.comment: The most common equivalent of ‘Lord’ is a term meaning ‘chief’ or ‘leader,’ but frequently this cannot be employed as a title for ‘God.’ One may, however, combine such an expression with a term for ‘God’ and employ a phrase meaning ‘God our leader’ or ‘God our chief.’ In some instances, however, a term for ‘Lord’ is related to a verb meaning ‘to command’ or ‘to order,’ and therefore ‘Lord’ is rendered as ‘the one who commands us’ and combined with ‘God’ may form a phrase such as ‘God, the one who commands us.’

senses.def: one who owns and controls property, including especially servants and slaves, with important supplementary semantic components of high status and respect
one who rules or exercises authority over others
senses.comment: For the meaning of κύριος as a title for God or for Christ, see 12.9.

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: a title of respect used in addressing or speaking of a man

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to his own master he stands or falls, probably a familiar adage) whether one maintains one’s status or relationship to a master depends on the master's judgment or evaluation
glosses: honor or disgrace depends on the person whom one serves

senses.def: largest of the great cats, often about 2.8 m from nose to tip of tail, standing as high as 1 m at the shoulder; pale yellowish brown in color; adult males have a mane around the neck and shoulders that is darker than the rest of their fur; Panthera leo; unclean animal; associated with aggression and strength
senses.comment: In some languages it may be important to use a descriptive phrase such as ‘a very large cat-like animal,’ though it will be important to try to make some distinction between ‘lion’ and ‘leopard’ (4.13). If necessary, some more extensive identification by description may be employed in a glossary.

senses.def: to reverse the result of tying by untying
to release from control, to set free (highly generic meaning applicable to a wide variety of circumstances, including confinement, political domination, sin, sickness)
senses.comment: In a number of languages there are problems with a somewhat literal translation of λυθῆναι ἀπὸ τοῦ δεσμοῦ τούτου in Luke 13:16 since the expression is highly figurative. The reference, of course, is to the woman’s condition as a cripple. Furthermore, it may not make sense to speak of ‘Satan binding’ such a person, as in the first part of verse 16. In a number of languages, therefore, one may speak of ‘Satan causing the woman to be a cripple,’ and then in the latter part of verse 16, one may speak of ‘causing a person no longer to be a cripple.’

senses.def: to destroy or reduce something to ruin by tearing down or breaking to pieces
senses.comment: In some languages there may be an important distinction in terms meaning ‘to destroy,’ depending upon whether the destruction is purposeful or not. A still further distinction may arise on the basis of beneficial or non-beneficial results. In Ephesians 2:14 the destruction is regarded as beneficial, while in Acts 27:41 the opposite is the case.

senses.def: to cause a gathering to be dismissed or dispersed
senses.comment: In some languages it may be more appropriate to render this expression in Acts 13:43 as ‘when most of the people had left’ or ‘when the meeting was over.’

senses.def: the failure to conform to a law or regulation, with a possible implication of regarding it as invalid
senses.comment: See also discussion at 36.29.

senses.def: to exercise authority over something on the basis of its being legitimate
senses.comment: There are a number of different interpretations of the implication of this statement in Matthew 16:19, and translators should carefully review this passage in various commentaries.

senses.def: to cause a state to cease
to cause to cease to exist
glosses: to cause to come to an end

senses.def: to beat severely with a whip
to punish severely, implying whipping
a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects
a position in the middle of an area (either an object in the midst of other objects or an area in the middle of a larger area)
a city on the south coast of Lycia in Asia Minor

senses.subdomain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About
senses.def: a reference to an entity, event, or state, clearly identified by the linguistic or non-linguistic context of the utterance
to make a loud cry as an expression of either joy or sorrow
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘cry aloud’ would simply be ‘scream.’ In this one occurrence of ὀλολύζω in the NT, the context refers to desperate circumstances, and one must often select an expression for ‘screaming’ or ‘crying’ which will be in keeping with this context referring to the threat of future misery.

senses.def: traditionally the measurement of a man’s arms stretched out horizontally, reckoned at approximately six feet or almost two meters and used as a technical, nautical term to measure the depth of water
senses.comment: If one adopts a metric system, the later expression in Acts 27:28, namely, ὀργυιὰς δεκαπέντε ‘fifteen fathoms,’ may be rendered as ‘about thirty meters.’

senses.def: a reference to an entity regarded as a part of the discourse setting, with pejorative meaning in certain contexts
a marker of an explanation or a clarification in the same or a different language
to act contrary to established custom or law, with the implication of intent
senses.comment: Languages differ appreciably in the way in which they speak of disobeying or transgressing a law. It is rarely possible to speak of ‘breaking a law,’ since nothing is actually done to the law in the process of transgression, but languages do employ such expressions as ‘to tramp on a law,’ ‘to ridicule a law,’ and ‘to laugh at a law.’ See also discussion at 36.29.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of παραβαίνω ‘to go aside,’ not occurring in the NT) to cease by removing oneself from some activity or position
senses.comment: In Acts 1:25 διακονίας and ἀποστολῆς are the events to which παρέβη is related as aspect.

senses.def: to cause to move along continually in the same direction as the force involved
(a figurative extension of meaning of παραφέρω[a] ‘to carry along,’ 15.162) to cause someone to depart from an earlier belief, with the implication of accepting a belief which is false
(an idiom, literally: to take the cup … from) to cause someone to not undergo some trying experience
glosses: to cause someone not to experience

senses.def: to cause something or someone to cease from some activity or state
to cease from an activity in which one is engaged
senses.comment: A literal rendering of Luke 5:4, however, may suggest a contradiction in some languages, since the initial clause implies a cessation of speech, while the principal clause indicates that Jesus spoke to Simon. It may be possible in some languages to use two entirely different words for speaking, one referring to speaking to a large group, and the second indicating a direct communication with a single person.

senses.def: to be left behind, with the implication of continuing to exist
to dispose of property or provide services in exchange for money or other valuable considerations
senses.comment: πιπράσκω and ἀποδίδομαι (ἀποδίδωμι[e]) may also be used to refer to selling a person into slavery. Note, for example, πιπράσκω in Matthew 18:25 (ἐκέλευσεν αὐτὸν ὁ κύριος πραθῆναι ‘his master ordered him to be sold as a slave’) and ἀποδίδομαι in Acts 7:9 (οἱ πατριάρχαι ζηλώσαντες τὸν Ἰωσὴφ ἀπέδοντο εἰς Αἴγυπτον ‘the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph and sold him to be a slave in Egypt’).|In a number of languages, however, it may be important to use a distinctive term for selling a person into slavery. In fact, it may be necessary to describe the event rather explicitly, for example, ‘to receive money for handing a person over to someone else to be a slave.’|In Romans 7:14 πιπράσκω is used figuratively in the phrase πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν ‘sold as a slave to sin,’ in the sense that sin is personified as the master.

senses.def: pertaining to that which exists in a variety of kinds
that which happens
an activity involving a measure of complexity and responsibility
legal action taken in a court of law against someone
senses.comment: In most languages there are technical terms for lawsuits or cases in court, but where these do not exist, one may always use a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘to accuse someone before a judge’ or ‘to argue against someone in court’ or ‘to say in court that someone has done a person harm.’

senses.def: to preach in anticipation or in advance
to take hold of or grasp, with focus upon the goal of the motion
senses.comment: In a number of languages quite different terms must be employed if one is to take someone by the hand in order to lead him or take someone by the hand in order to rescue him. The difference implied in the presumed force or strength required frequently results in quite different words being used.|The phrase προσλαμβάνομαι τροφῆς (Acts 27:36) may be interpreted as an idiom meaning ‘to eat’ (see footnote at μετέχω 23.2).

senses.def: to take or bring along in addition to oneself
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret προσλαμβάνομαι in Acts 17:5 as meaning ‘to gather together’ (see 15.127).

senses.def: to take or lead off to oneself
gather together to oneself a group of persons
senses.comment: It is also possible that προσλαμβάνομαι in Acts 17:5 means ‘to take along in addition to oneself’ (see 15.167).

senses.def: to accept the presence of a person with friendliness
any kind of bird, wild or domestic
senses.comment: All languages have at least some terms for birds, but there may be no generic term which identifies birds while excluding all other creatures which fly. For example, in some languages a term which includes all kinds of birds also includes flying insects and bats. However, since in most instances such a term has birds as its primary reference, it can usually be employed in contexts in which birds are more or less readily identified by other expressions in the passage. In other languages generic terms for birds may identify only certain classes of birds, for example, birds of prey, water birds, and birds of the forest.

senses.def: a city on a promontory in the south of Italy
large board or plank of wood
mustard plant, a large herb noted for its very small seeds and in some instances growing to a height of three meters (about ten feet)
senses.comment: Note that in Matthew 13:31 (and in the parallel passage Luke 13:19) σίναπι is actually spoken of as a δένδρον tree, evidently a type of rhetorical hyperbole.|Though the mustard plant may not be known in certain areas of the world, the use of mustard as a condiment is widely known, and therefore it is often possible to speak of ‘a plant that produces mustard’ or ‘the plant used in making mustard.’ In order, however, to make the parable meaningful, it may be necessary to have some explanation of this plant in a footnote or glossary.

senses.def: a follower of Jesus
secondary projection from the trunk or bough of a tree or shrub, with its leaves attached
to toil together with someone in a struggle, implying opposition and/or competition

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
senses.def: a point of time marking the end of a duration
senses.comment: As in the case of a number of expressions involving ‘end,’ it may be important to use a verb meaning ‘to finish,’ for example, ‘so it will be like that when the age finishes’ or ‘… when there isn’t any more of the age.’

senses.def: to have understanding about practical matters and thus be able to act sensibly
senses.comment: It is also possible to understand σωφρονισμός in 2 Timothy 1:7 as moderation and sensible behavior (see 88.93).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to behave in a sensible manner, with the implication of thoughtful awareness of what is best
senses.comment: For another interpretation of σωφρονισμός in 2 Timothy 1:7, see 32.34.

senses.def: cardinal number, where there are forty instances of a countable entity

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a very long period of time
senses.comment: Though most translations render ἔτη τεσσεράκοντα as ‘forty years,’ the expression probably is to be understood as meaning an unusually long period of time. See also discussion at 67.93.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (literally: forty days and forty nights) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
senses.comment: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (shortened form of [c] literally, forty days) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
senses.comment: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

senses.def: a district to the south of Damascus
pertaining to being wet or moist

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: any type of footwear (though ordinarily the reference would be to a sandal rather than to a shoe)
a title used as a proper name of the Egyptian king
to cause the process of burning to begin
senses.comment: As already noted in the series of terms listed in 14.63, languages differ appreciably in terms employed for different phases and results of burning. For example, to set something on fire for the sake of providing warmth may be expressed by quite a different term from that which is used in speaking of the process of setting something on fire in order to destroy it.

senses.def: pertaining to being well lighted
senses.comment: In a number of languages one cannot speak of an object being ‘full of light,’ for light is not spoken of as a substance. It is, of course, normally possible to speak of something as ‘having light inside’ (for example, the occurrence of light within a room). However, rather than speaking positively of the occurrence of light, it is sometimes more satisfactory to indicate the absence of darkness, for example, ‘there was no darkness there’ or, as in Matthew 6:22, ‘your whole body will have no darkness in it.’

senses.def: pertaining to being bright or shining, either of a source or of an object which is illuminated by a source
any kind of food or nourishment
senses.comment: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as Matthew 6:11 as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering Luke 4:4 (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of Luke 4:4 is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

senses.def: the essence of life in terms of thinking, willing, and feeling
senses.comment: It is also possible to render ψυχή in Philippians 1:27 as ‘purpose’ or ‘desire,’ for ψυχή focuses upon the total psychological being involved in struggling for the faith.|ψυχή[a] is often glossed as ‘heart’ or ‘desire.’ Compare the following: περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου ‘my heart is sorrowful even to the point of death’ Matthew 26:38; ἵνα μὴ κάμητε ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν ἐκλυόμενοι ‘so do not let your hearts become discouraged and give up’ Hebrews 12:3 (for ψυχή in the idiom κάμνω τῇ ψυχῇ, see 25.291); ἀλλ ὡς δοῦλοι Χριστοῦ ποιοῦντες τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκ ψυχῆς ‘but with all your heart, do what God wants, as slaves of Christ’ Ephesians 6:6. In these passages, however, ψυχή refers really to the entire being of a person, so that Matthew 26:38 may very well be rendered as ‘my sorrow is so great it almost kills me.’ Hebrews 12:3 may also be rendered as ‘so do not let yourselves be discouraged and give up,’ and Ephesians 6:6 may be appropriately rendered as ‘but with your whole being, do what God wants, as slaves of Christ.’|The meaning of ψυχή in the sense of the person as an individual is treated under ψυχή[c] (9.20) as, for example, in Matthew 11:29 (εὑρήσετε ἀνάπαυσιν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν ‘you will find rest for yourselves’).|Even in those contexts in which ψυχή refers to existence beyond death, it may be referring figuratively to the person. For example, in Acts 2:27 (οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μου εἰς ᾅδην one may translate ‘you will not abandon my soul to Hades’ or ‘you will not abandon me to the grave.’|It is important to distinguish ψυχή[a], signifying a psychological faculty, from ψυχή[b], meaning ‘physical life, life principle’ (23.88). Note, for example, the occurrence of ψυχή[b] in Hebrews 4:12 (διϊκνούμενος ἄχρι μερισμοῦ ψυχῆς καὶ πνεύματος ‘it cuts all the way through to where physical life and spirit meet’). Note also the occurrence of ψυχή[b] in 1 Thessalonians 5:23 αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς, καὶ ὁλόκληρον ὑμῶν τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τὸ σῶμα ἀμέμπτως ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τηρηθείη ‘may the God who gives us peace make you holy in every way and keep your whole being - spirit, life, and body - free from all fault at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ’).|In certain contexts ψυχή would appear to be in contrast with καρδία (26.3) and διάνοια (26.14) as, for example, in Matthew 22:37 ἀγαπήσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου ἐν ὅλω τῇ καρδίᾳ σου καὶ ἐν ὅλω τῇ ψυχῇ σου καὶ ἐν ὅλω τῇ διανοίᾳ σου ‘you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and soul and mind’). Because of the three terms, some have insisted that there must be at least three quite different parts of human personality. Others, however, have concluded that instead of being three parts of personality, these are only three different perspectives which one may employ in thinking about or describing human personality. Still others would contend that the use of the three terms, καρδία, ψυχή and διάνοια, only emphasizes the totality of human personality, and no clear-cut distinctions can possibly be made. Certainly the referents involve considerable overlapping. One could translate with complete justification Matthew 22:37 as ‘you shall love the Lord with all your heart and life and mind.’ In fact, in many languages it is impossible to distinguish between καρδία, ψυχή, and διάνοια, and therefore it may be necessary to translate as ‘you shall love the Lord your God with all that you desire and with all that you think’ or ‘you must love the Lord your God with all your being.’

senses.def: the existence of a human being, or other living creature, sustained by the presence of air to breathe and food to eat
senses.comment: In rendering ψυχή in Romans 11:3 it may be necessary to indicate more precisely the relationship between ‘to seek’ and ‘life,’ for example, ‘they seek to destroy my life’ or ‘they seek to cause me no longer to live.’|In a number of languages there is no noun-like word for ‘life.’ It may therefore be necessary to change all passages which speak of ‘life’ into a corresponding expression using a verb-like form meaning ‘to live.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ψυχή[a] ‘inner self, mind,’ 26.4) a person as a living being
(an idiom, literally: living soul) any living creature, whether animal or human
senses.comment: Though the phrase ψυχὴ ζωῆς is highly generic in meaning, its specific reference in Revelation 16:3 is to creatures of the sea, and therefore in most languages one must translate simply ‘fish’ or ‘that which lives in the sea.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to be tormented in soul) to experience mental torment involving sorrow mixed with anger
glosses: to be tormented in one’s heart

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to cause a person’s attitude to be bad against) to cause someone to have hostile feelings of dislike toward someone
(an idiom, literally: to become tired in spirit) to gradually lose one’s motivation to accomplish some goal

senses.subdomain: Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to acquire one’s soul or to acquire one’s life) to save oneself from grave danger or death
(an idiom, literally: to hand over life) to expose oneself willingly to a danger or risk
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘risking one’s life’ is ‘exposing oneself to death’ or ‘showing that one is willing to die’ or ‘walking into the danger of dying.’

senses.subdomain: Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to do something with regard to one’s life) to save or preserve one’s own life
(an idiom, literally: a sword goes through one’s soul) to feel the intense pain of sorrow
(an idiom, literally: to lay down one’s life) to die, with the implication of voluntary or willing action
senses.comment: Though in English the phrases ‘to lay down one’s life’ or ‘to give one’s life’ do suggest a voluntary dying, a literal rendering of such expressions in other languages would not necessarily imply the same. It may therefore be necessary to use such expressions as ‘to die willingly’ or ‘to die without resisting.’ In some languages ‘willingly’ is expressed primarily as a negation of objecting, for example, ‘I will not object to dying.’
